Test error, rentals/day939

What we measured

731 days of real rental data; 28 days used to establish history; 611 development days and 92 final test days. Every prediction uses information available just after the preceding day closes. The final test covers October–December 2012.

The selected model was chosen on three earlier validation windows. All model settings were locked before inspecting the final test. MAE is the average absolute miss in rental counts; it is not a percentage accuracy score.

model MAE RMSE MAE_improvement_pct selected_before_test

Ridge 938.97 1379.68 35.58 True
Gradient boosting 1374.16 1887.31 5.72 False

The calendar-only model is an explanatory comparison. Reported performance is limited to this historical period; it does not demonstrate current-system performance or operational savings.

How to learn from this project

Read the walkthrough below, then open the notebook to change code and rerun it. Keep the final test results fixed when reporting this experiment; later changes are exploratory unless tested on new data.

Tomorrow’s bikes: a first forecasting project

Question: Can calendar information and past rental counts predict the next day’s total Capital Bikeshare rentals better than using the same weekday last week?

A forecast could inform staffing and maintenance planning. We do not measure operational savings or station-level shortages. This is a historical learning project, not a deployed forecast service.

Start here: Run the cells in order from the extracted project folder. The supporting project.py contains the fully commented modeling functions. Everything runs on a CPU; no API keys are needed.

Vocabulary: A row is one day. The target is the number we want to predict (cnt). Features are the clues we provide to a model. Training means learning a relationship from past examples. A baseline is a simple rule our model should beat.

1. Gather and audit the data

Source: UCI Bike Sharing. We use the daily file, not the hourly file. There are 731 calendar days from January 2011 through December 2012. The data are bundled for offline reruns; the code downloads them from UCI if absent.

We check for missing cells, repeated dates, missing calendar days, negative counts and inconsistent totals. Cleaning should respond to actual problems: a clean dataset does not need invented imputation or arbitrary outlier removal.

2. Define exactly when we forecast

For a target day t, issue the forecast just after day t−1 closes. We assume that complete prior-day counts are immediately available. This is not an earlier-evening forecast.

We use known calendar information and past counts. We exclude target-day weather: this dataset records what the weather actually was, not what a forecast predicted. We also exclude casual and registered, since those add up to the answer we are trying to predict.

During evaluation, yesterday’s observed count becomes available before today’s prediction. Model coefficients remain fixed throughout the test. This simulates repeated daily forecasts; it is not a forecast of all three months made on September 30.

3. Make features without looking into the future

A lag is a previous observation: lag_7 means rentals seven days earlier. A rolling mean averages a recent window. We shift counts back one day *before* computing rolling statistics, so today’s answer cannot enter today’s features.

Calendar inputs are weekday, holiday, working-day indicator, seasonal sine/cosine and elapsed time. Sine/cosine represent the annual cycle smoothly, keeping December and January close together. History inputs are counts 1, 7 and 14 days ago, prior 7- and 28-day averages, and prior 7-day variability.

We drop the first 28 days because they lack a complete history window. All later days, including unusual days, remain.

4. Separate learning from the final exam

The development set contains dates before October 1, 2012. The test set is October–December 2012. We never shuffle dates: forecasting requires learning from the past and predicting the future.

Within development data, we use three practice exams (validation folds). Each uses a longer training history followed by 60 later validation days. Model settings are selected by average validation error. The test is consulted only after the choices have been saved.

This plan and the small candidate grids were written in EXPERIMENT_PLAN.md before fitting any models.

test = data.loc[data.dteday >= p.CUTOFF].copy()

5. Train a baseline and two models

- Last-week baseline: predict the same count as seven days ago. No training is needed.
- Ridge regression: learns a weighted combination of the clues. A regularization penalty discourages unstable, excessively large weights. Numeric scaling is fitted on training data only.
- Gradient boosting: combines many small decision trees, each correcting some remaining errors. It can learn more flexible patterns than a weighted sum.
- Calendar-only Ridge: a separate explanatory comparison, removing rental history to test whether it adds value. It is not eligible for the primary selection.

We try four Ridge penalties and two boosting tree counts. MAE (mean absolute error) is the average size of a miss in rentals per day. Lower is better. RMSE penalizes especially large misses more heavily. The primary candidate with the lowest validation MAE is selected—even if that turns out to be the baseline.

6. Evaluate the locked choices on unseen dates

The learned models are fitted once on all development data. For each test day, we supply only calendar information and already-completed daily counts. We do not change features, settings or the selected model after seeing these results.

The MAE improvement column compares each method with the last-week baseline. A positive value means less error. The selected model may not be the best in the final test; that is useful evidence about stability, not a reason to retune on the test.

Code and recorded outputs
metrics, predictions, failures = p.evaluate(test, models, winner)
print(metrics.round(2).to_string(index=False))
selected = metrics.loc[metrics.model.eq(winner)].iloc[0]
print(f'\nSelected model: {winner}; test MAE = {selected.MAE:.1f} rentals/day; improvement = {selected.MAE_improvement_pct:.1f}%.')
p.plot_results(metrics, predictions, winner)
plt.show()

7. Understand failures, not just the average

Large misses are part of the result. The plots and table identify difficult days without deleting them. A calendar-plus-history model can struggle with abrupt changes and unusual conditions. This analysis does not establish the cause of any individual miss.

The weekday/weekend breakdown checks whether average performance hides different behavior on those groups; public holidays are not reclassified as weekends.

8. What this does and does not establish

This experiment measures forecast error on 92 historical days from one bike-share system. These are observed rentals, not all potential demand: unavailable bicycles can suppress observed counts. We cannot claim station-level availability improvements, financial savings, causal effects or performance in a modern bike-share system.

There are only two annual cycles. The holdout contains autumn and early winter, not a full future year. We omit forecast weather because no historical weather forecasts are provided. The last completed daily count is assumed promptly available. Future work could add genuine weather forecasts and evaluate on several more years, with a new untouched test period.

Once this test has been examined, it cannot serve as an untouched test for later redesigns. Any further feature experiments must be labeled exploratory or evaluated on new held-out data.

9. Exploratory extensions: what we learned next

The original test has already been inspected. The following analyses are exploratory and do not replace the original result or create a fresh test set. The extension plan is in EXTENSION_PLAN.md. Every original prediction remains unchanged.

### Which information helps?

We add history-only Ridge to the calendar-only and combined versions. Each version tunes its penalty using the same three earlier validation windows. History-only performs similarly to the combined version. This suggests recent counts carry much of the signal in this experiment, but does not establish that calendar information is always unhelpful.

### How uncertain is the improvement?

We resample blocks of adjacent test days, keeping baseline and Ridge errors paired. We use 10,000 samples with seven-day blocks, and check three- and fourteen-day blocks. The 95% percentile interval describes approximate uncertainty conditional on this historical test period and the fitted models. It is not an interval for tomorrow's rental count. A short, changing season and unmodeled training uncertainty limit the interpretation.

### Does recent volatility warn of mistakes?

Volatility is the preceding seven-day standard deviation divided by its mean. We flag days above the development-period 75th percentile. Validation folds use thresholds learned only on each fold's earlier training data. These diagnostics share the original model-selection data and are descriptive. No threshold is optimized against the test results.

10. Visual evidence for the exploratory analyses

The feature comparison shows very similar errors for history-only and combined Ridge. The bootstrap distribution remains above zero for most or all displayed draws, with the percentile interval above zero for every checked block length. That supports an advantage within this period, not a guarantee across other systems or years.

Higher recent volatility is associated with higher average errors. Yet the warning fails to flag October 29, the first shutdown day. A warning based on past counts can lag a sudden disruption.

11. Context for the largest failures

Sandy, October 29–30: ARLnow's October 31 reporting describes an approximately 36-hour Capital Bikeshare suspension and reopening on Tuesday afternoon. The model predicted 5,862 rentals on October 29, while the dataset records 22. Service availability is a plausible and directly documented part of the explanation. It does not establish why exactly 22 rentals appear in this dataset.

December 24: The National Weather Service documents rain in the Washington DC metro. The source data mark the date as a working day, despite its position in the holiday period. Holiday effects remain a hypothesis.

December 26: The NWS documents winter weather in northern Virginia, including Arlington and Fairfax, on December 26–27. This is regional context, not proof of the causal contribution of weather or a full-system closure.

All days remain in the reported scores. Observed rentals reflect service availability as well as demand. These sources do not become model inputs. A future study needs archived weather forecasts and service announcements with publication timestamps.

Sources and detailed qualifications are in EVENT_CONTEXT.md:

12. Conclusions to explain in your presentation

1. The original combined Ridge model reduces final-test MAE from 1,458 to 939 rentals/day, a 35.6% reduction.
2. The exploratory history-only model performs similarly. We keep the original selected model and distinguish this later comparison.
3. The seven-day block-bootstrap 95% interval for improvement is approximately 21.1%–49.7%, conditional on the period and fitted models.
4. Past volatility gives an imperfect warning. It misses the onset of the Sandy shutdown.
5. Service notices and archived weather forecasts are promising future inputs, requiring new test dates.
